subtitle.en: Scholar of Islam on the Kenya Coast

meta.en: Role: Associate Professor of Islamic Studies, Department of Philosophy and Religious Studies, Pwani University; Secretary of the Digo Ngambi (traditional leadership council)
Region: Kenya coast — teaches at Pwani University, Kilifi; serves the Digo community of Kwale
Field: Islamic studies, focused on how colonial and post-colonial states have dealt with Islam, and on religion and politics in Kenya

blocks.en: In the academic study of Islam in East Africa, a small number of scholars have done the painstaking work of recovering the institutional history of Muslim communities on the Kenya coast — the kadhi courts, the mosques, the Muslim councils and the political movements through which coastal Muslims have negotiated their place in the Kenyan state. Hassan Mwakimako is among the most productive of them, and he is also an officer of the Digo community's own revived leadership council.
Academic Career

Mwakimako earned his PhD in the Department of Religious Studies at the **University of Cape Town** in 2003, on a fellowship from the Universities Science, Humanities and Engineering Partnerships in Africa (USHEPIA) programme. He was then on study leave from the **University of Nairobi**, his home institution at the time. His supervisors were Abdulkader Tayob and Muhammad Bakari. In spring 2002 he spent a term as a fellow of the Institute for the Study of Islamic Thought in Africa (ISITA) at Northwestern University [1].

He went on to a postdoctoral research fellowship at the Zentrum Moderner Orient (ZMO) in Berlin. In 2016–17 he was an African Studies Visiting Fellow at the Centre of African Studies, University of Cambridge [2][3].

He is now **Associate Professor of Islamic Studies** in the Department of Philosophy and Religious Studies at **Pwani University** in Kilifi [2][4]. Working from a coastal university matters. Much Kenyan academic research on Islam has come from Nairobi, at some distance from the communities it studies. Mwakimako, who began his career in Nairobi, now works from inside the region whose history he documents. He also lectures abroad: in September 2025 he gave a lecture at Utrecht University titled "Islam, Muslims and Governance in East Africa" [5].

His research interests are the meeting point of colonial and post-colonial state policy with Islam, religion and politics, and contemporary Islam [2]. His work has appeared with Edinburgh University Press, Brill, Amsterdam University Press and Lit Verlag. It has also appeared in journals including *Islam and Christian–Muslim Relations*, *Religion Compass*, *Islamic Africa* and the *Journal of Eastern African Studies* [4][6][7][8][9].
The Kadhis and the Colonial State

Mwakimako's doctoral thesis is titled *Politics, Ethnicity and Jostling for Power: The Evolution of Institutions of Muslim Leadership and Kadhiship in Colonial Kenya, 1895–1963* (2003). It traces who the British appointed as Shaykh al-Islam, Chief Kadhi and town kadhis in Mombasa, Nairobi and Mumias. It argues that colonial officials preferred *ulama* (Islamic scholars) of Arab descent, which created the impression that non-Arab Muslims were not qualified for these posts. In his words, this turned "a religious form of authority into prevalent racialized politics". Loyalty to colonial policy and the racial identity of the appointee mattered more than learning [1].
The thesis does not focus on the Digo. Even so, it helps explain Digo history: the Digo were among the African Muslims of the coast who were passed over by that system.
Key Publications
His publication record spans two decades and includes:
***Politics, Ethnicity and Jostling for Power*** (PhD thesis, University of Cape Town, 2003) — the foundation of his work on Muslim leadership in colonial Kenya [1].
**"The ulama and the colonial state in the protectorate of Kenya"** (2006), in *The Global Worlds of the Swahili* (Lit Verlag, Berlin) [6].
***Mosques in Kenya: Muslim Opinions on Religion, Politics and Development*** (Klaus Schwarz Verlag, Berlin, 2007) [6].

**"Christian–Muslim Relations in Kenya: A Catalogue of Events and Meanings"** (*Islam and Christian–Muslim Relations* 18(2), 2007) — a systematic mapping of interfaith relations, from colonial history and the independence struggle to constitutional debates over the kadhi courts [6][10].
**"Kadhi Court and Appointment of Kadhi in Kenya Colony"** (*Religion Compass* 2(4), 2008) — how British rule restructured Islamic judicial authority on the coast [6].
**"Conflicts and Tensions in the Appointment of Chief Kadhi in Colonial Kenya"** (2010), in *Muslim Family Law in Sub-Saharan Africa* (Amsterdam University Press) [7].

**"Islam, Politics and Violence on the Kenya Coast"** (with Justin Willis, 2014) — a policy note written after the Mpeketoni attack. It examines how developments within coastal Islam, wider movements of political Islam, and secular grievance and political ambition combine to make the coast volatile [11].

**"Islam and Democracy: Debating Electoral Involvement on the Kenya Coast"** (with Justin Willis, *Islamic Africa* 7(1), Brill, 2016) — on the debate among coastal Muslims about whether to take part in elections. Around the 2013 election some mosque speakers urged a boycott. The article asks what that debate reveals about the relationship between Islam and democracy in Kenya [8][12].

**"Preaching Politics: Islam and Christianity on the Kenya Coast"** (with Gregory Deacon, George Gona and Justin Willis, *Journal of Contemporary African Studies* 35(2), 2017) — a comparative study of how the two faiths engage with public political life on the coast [13].

**"Integrationism vs. Rejectionism: Revisiting the History of Islamist Activism in Coastal Kenya"** (with Jannis Saalfeld, *Journal of Eastern African Studies* 17(1–2), 2023) — contrasts the Islamic Party of Kenya, which worked through elections, with the Ansar Sunnah movement, which rejected them [9].

Co-editor, with Farouk Topan, Kai Kresse and Erin E. Stiles, of ***Governance and Islam in East Africa: Muslims and the State*** (Edinburgh University Press with the Aga Khan University Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations, 2024). The open-access volume has thirteen case studies on Muslims and the state in Kenya and Tanzania [4][14]. His own chapter in it is **"The Supreme Council of Kenya Muslims (SUPKEM): Jostling for Representativeness among Muslims in Kenya"**. It traces SUPKEM from its founding in the 1970s through the leadership contests of the 1990s [15].
The Ngambi Role

Beyond academia, Mwakimako serves as **Secretary** of the Digo Ngambi, the traditional leadership council the Digo community revived in 2023. The leadership was announced on 2 October 2023. Former Cabinet Minister Chirau Ali Mwakwere was named spokesman, former Msambweni MP Marere wa Mwachai deputy, and Mwakimako secretary [16][17].

Mwakimako spoke to the press for the new council. He told journalists that in the past the Digo community had its traditional rulers and leaders through the Ngambi, and that the community was reviving that institution for the sake of cultural revival [16]. He also gave the wider case for it: "There is nothing wrong with the Digo having a traditional authority, just as is the case with other communities like the Kikuyu and the Luo, to ensure the protection and preservation of their traditions." He presented the council as the end of years of disunity: "We must unite as a community for us to be respected by others and make an impact on the country's political and socio-economic scene" [16][17].

He then chaired the **Coronation Committee** for Mwakwere's installation as Digo spokesperson, held in traditional regalia at Kwale Baraza Park on 28 October 2023, with Digo cultural dances. At the ceremony he announced plans for a Digo cultural event that December. Kaya elders also asked Mwakwere to push for official recognition of the Digo as a community in their own right, rather than only as part of the Mijikenda [18].

The Ngambi's position within the wider Mijikenda is still being settled. In July 2026, elders from the nine kayas publicly rejected Mwakwere's later installation as spokesman for all the Mijikenda [19]. That dispute concerns the wider Mijikenda title, not the Digo Ngambi itself, and no report links Mwakimako to it.

Mwakimako combines academic authority with an office in the community's own leadership. His research on how colonial and post-colonial states have engaged with Muslim communities on the coast bears directly on the structures the Digo community now has to deal with.
Research Collaborators

Mwakimako has published with a network of scholars of the Kenya coast and of Islam in East Africa. They include the historian Justin Willis of Durham University, Gregory Deacon, George Gona and Jannis Saalfeld, and his co-editors Farouk Topan, Kai Kresse and Erin E. Stiles [4][9][11][12][13]. Together with other recent scholars, this network has taken the field beyond the older generation of Western historians of the coast (Sperling, Pouwels) and towards coast-based analysis.
Legacy

Mwakimako's published work covers Islam on the Kenya coast as a whole rather than Digo history in particular. Still, his scholarship and his community role make him important to the effort to document and advocate for Digo cultural identity. He has spent two decades studying how coastal Muslim communities have been governed, marginalised and represented. As Secretary of the Digo Ngambi, he is now helping the community represent itself.
